summary: Return the number of nodes on the shortest root-to-LEAF path.
mainInsight: The minimum depth ends at the nearest leaf (a node with no children), not at the first missing child. Level-order BFS finds it as soon as it meets the first leaf, without exploring deeper levels.
canonicalApproach: BFS level order with early exit

approaches.name: Recursive DFS
approaches.summary: If one child is missing, use the other child's depth; else 1 + min(left, right).

approaches.name: BFS level order with early exit
approaches.summary: Return the level of the first leaf found.

personalSolution.approach: BFS level order with early exit

promptVariants: Why is BFS a good fit for the minimum depth?
Which traversal finds the nearest leaf first?
options: Level-order BFS: the first leaf met is the shallowest
cards.answer: Level-order BFS: the first leaf met is the shallowest
cards.explanation: BFS visits nodes by increasing depth, so it can stop at the first leaf.

incorrectOptionExplanations.Preorder DFS: May explore deep branches before finding a shallow leaf.

promptVariants: Why is `1 + min(left depth, right depth)` wrong for nodes with only one child?
What does the minimum depth require at the end of the path?
cards.answer: A missing child is not a leaf: for a node with one child, min(0, d) = 0 would stop at that node even though it is not a leaf. The path must end at a leaf, so with one child you must follow the existing child; only when both children exist is min() appropriate.
keyPoints: Path must end at a leaf
Single-child node is not a leaf

promptVariants: Complete the statement: Worst-case time complexity: ___
cards.explanation: In the worst case (e.g. a complete tree where leaves are on the last level) all nodes are visited.

promptVariants: What is the BFS memory and when is it large?
How does BFS space compare with DFS recursion?
cards.answer: BFS stores one level at a time: O(w), up to about n/2 for a complete tree. DFS uses O(h), which is O(log n) when balanced but O(n) for a skewed tree.

promptVariants: Your queue also enqueues None children and you check `if node and ...`. What is the effect and how would you tidy it?
Why does the level counter increase per while-iteration?
cards.answer: Each outer iteration processes exactly one level, so ans counts levels (depth). Enqueuing None children adds useless work and requires the `if node` guards; only enqueue existing children: `if node.left: queue.append(node.left)`. The first leaf encountered ends the search.
cards.explanation: The early return is the BFS advantage.

promptVariants: What is the minimum depth of the left-skewed tree 2 -> 3 -> 4 (all left children)?
cards.explanation: Node 2 is not a leaf because it has a child, so the path must continue to the leaf 4.

incorrectOptionExplanations.1: The root is not a leaf.
